## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting architecture scored 0/0. I read its code. The observation has 4Z+3 channels (27 for this world). The action layout is type-major: type × Y·X anchor cells, then DONE as the last index. Footprints come from spec. The default budget allows only 32 updates of 4096 steps, which is very few for an exact-build task with 6–16 bricks that depends on placement order. One footprint-pooled feature costs about 50k MACs per cell, so a network of similar cost keeps r≤1. Fewer PPO epochs could give about 3.25x more samples. My guess is that the zero comes mainly from too few samples and weak credit assignment, plus a placement head that cannot directly compare all cells under a footprint jointly. The design: A and B share a new architecture and differ only in epochs. B and C share a recipe and differ only in architecture. That separates the effect of the recipe from the effect of the architecture.

### Round 2
All three trials scored 0 on dev and 0 on training success. Seeds made no difference. Neither 1 nor 2 PPO epochs helped, and neither did ~3x more samples or either spatial head (footprint conv or pooling). These trials changed almost everything except one shared assumption: every head, including the starting one, outputs a [types, Y, X] map that is flattened type-major with a top-left anchor. If this world's real action layout differs (cell-major, transposed or a different anchor), every spatial head is scrambled. That would explain why even the shaping reward was never exploited enough to give any training success. This round tests that directly with layout-agnostic heads. A learned dense map from per-cell conv features to every action can learn any layout, so the conv trunk still provides translation-equivariant local features. A hybrid (spatial + dense) covers the case where the layout is fine. A third run checks epoch sensitivity for the dense head.

### Round 3
All six trials scored 0 on dev and 0 on training success. That covers spatial and dense heads, 1, 2 and 4 epochs, and 220k to 430k steps. The dense head did no better, so a mislabelled action layout alone probably doesn't explain the zeros. The likelier cause is that the network cannot easily compute where a brick lands. A placement is good only if, at the landing layer (the highest build height under the footprint), every covered cell is missing and nothing below gets sealed in. Mixing the Z layers into channels at the first layer makes that comparison hard to learn. The reward also favours big bricks that are only partly correct. So this round tests a layer-token design. Each (layer z, cell) gets its own token holding the full column, slices for layers z-1, z and z+1, and a one-hot of z. A learned footprint convolution scores each brick at each layer, and logsumexp over layers picks one score. The candidates vary the recipe and add spatial context.

### Round 4
All 9 trials scored exactly 0, on dev and in training. That includes spatial heads, dense heads, layer-token heads, 1 or 2 PPO epochs, and gammas from 0.99 to 0.995. Differences in compute and recipe changed nothing. The dense head can learn any action layout, but it is too slow to learn: 450k parameters, each row trained only by its own rare actions. Even stochastic training never produced one exact build. That pattern fits a world whose action layout differs from its description, such as transposed or flipped anchors, cell-major order, or DONE first. It also fits plain difficulty. This is the last round, so I hedge structurally. A shared conv trunk feeds several cheap 1x1 heads, and each head emits its logits under a different fixed reindexing. The heads' contributions are summed or gated, so gradient favours whichever layout is real. The identity layout is still included, so the described case stays covered.
